answer.rationale: memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory here: it is the only record that says moving primary supply to the low-cost vendor worked, and it is the sole justification for the one action (full switch) that satisfies the 18% mandate on its own. So it is the one worth spending the verification budget on. What the consolidated line does not tell me is context that decides whether the analogy holds: was that switch on a component of comparable volume and criticality, was there finished-goods or raw buffer absorbing the qualification period, and how long was 'quick onboarding' in actual days? At 94% of committed volume with zero buffer and 14 days to expiry, a wholesale primary switch converts a price win into an unhedged delivery bet — exactly the risk the objective forbids increasing. memory_c1 and memory_c6 support incumbent continuity but memory_c4's renegotiation lever is dead this cycle (price refused), and memory_c5's defer pattern is unsafe because this contract does not auto-renew, so drift means a supply lapse rather than a month-to-month glide. The best-supported move is memory_c3's pattern: qualify the low-cost vendor as a second source at guarded volume — a small share that proves their quality, lead time and allocation behavior against live demand — paired with a short bridge/extension on the incumbent line so primary supply never lapses. This captures a partial cost reduction now and buys the evidence needed to escalate. I flag explicitly that this will NOT hit the full 18% this year; that gap is a real cost to report to finance rather than something to close by taking on unbounded line-down risk. If the archive shows memory_c2 came from a comparable-criticality, comparable-volume part with no buffer cushion, I would upgrade toward a phased full switch at the next review; if it shows a low-volume or well-buffered part, the guarded second source stays the ceiling and the mandate shortfall gets renegotiated at the portfolio level.
